Given the right scenario, frequency will converge to expected value.
We use this principle to estimate the accuracy of classification.

0-1 loss is a measure on classification performance its counting the off diagonal entries in a confusion matrix

in the long run we want to minimize the expected loss. 

If the true label $k$ is the same as the estimated label $\hat{G}$ then the 0-1 loss value is 0
if the true label and estimated label are different then the loss value is 1

$L(G(x), \hat{G}(X))$ The G(x) value is random in the bayesean framework (but in frequentist its deterministic) in general $\hat{G}(x)$ is also random every time.

The minimizer, fortunately to minimize the expected 0-1 loss we can just minimize everything after the $E_X$

Bayesans make decisions based on maximum post posterior probability.

Deep learning at a simple level follows a similar principle where once you minimize entropy loss you basically end up minimizing 0-1 loss anyway.

0-1 loss doesn't always work when the structure of loss is not symmetric.
The threshold of 0.5 doesn't always work if there is an imbalance in the consequences of false negative vs false positive

if you change the threshold you likely aren't using 0-1 loss anymore.

When using bayes classifier multi-class the process is mostly the same, except that it has different thresholds for class assignment based on posterior probability

In classification there are many methods, but the Bayes method is the peak

## 4A
#### k-nearest neighbor (kNN)

Nearest Neighbor Methods
- a class of classification methods and belong to the family of supervised learning methods, where methods are trained from observations that have class labels
- classify a new observation to a class using features of its neighboring observations
- can be regarded as estimating the unknown conditional probabilities that are used by the Bayes classifier.

In our case we always measure a fixed number of features and worth with that exact number, in the real world this is not always the case.

KNN algorithm:
1. Specify a positive integer k as the number of neighbors
1. Let $K_N(X)$ be the neighborhood of x consisting of $k$ points $x_i$. Compute the average label as $\bar{Y}$.
1. Specify a threshold $\beta\in(0,1)$ and estimate the class label of $x$ as $\hat{Y} = 1 \text{ if } \bar{Y}(x) > \beta \text{ or } \bar{Y}(x) = 0 \text{ otherwise.}$

See time series: moving average operator ~ convolution ~ blur imaging

Your neighborhood changes shape as you move it no matter how dense or sparsely populated your observations are.
You don't always have to use $\frac{1}{K}$ for the weights of your observations. Sometimes it can be worth weighting them by distance from the point you are examining.

The average label will be 0 or 1 when either a. all neighbors are 0 or 1 b. there is only 1 neighbor.

in the Bayesian scheme you set $\beta = \frac{1}{2}$ and use the $\frac{1}{k}$ to approximate Bayes rule.
The average function is an unbiased estimator of $Pr(Y_i = 1)$, in other words the average is estimating the probability that the class label is 1.

In the real world, all we have is frequency. We never have a real idea of what the actual probabilities are going to be. Take weather prediction, we don't know when its going to rain but we know the past frequency of rain.

A kNN method needs:
- a neighborhood size $k$
- a measure of whether two observations are "close"
- a threshold on the "average label" to make a decision.
kNN is non-parametric, it does not assume a distribution for the observations.
Unless otherwise noted, Euclidean distance will be used to measure how close the observations are and when there are 2 classes the threshold on the average label will be 0.5
